hypothesis: If Thompson is right, the constant (equiangular) angle of the logarithmic spiral fitted to typical helicospiral gastropod shells is almost never below 80° and mostly between 80° and 85°.
pass_criterion: Using S_Table_3_hangle_output.csv (and S_Table_1/2 for taxon metadata), convert the fitted per-specimen whorl expansion rate W to the spiral angle alpha = arctan(2π / ln W) (per whorl), after excluding non-typical shells (flat, planispiral or very depressed forms). The claim passes if, among typical helicospiral specimens, at least 90% have alpha >= 80° and at least 50% have alpha in [80°, 85°], with a median between 80° and 85°.
fail_criterion: The claim fails if fewer than 80% of typical specimens have alpha >= 80°, or if the median alpha lies outside 78°–87°, or if fewer than 33% fall in [80°, 85°].
interpretation: Thompson's "constant angle" is the angle between the radius vector and the tangent of the equiangular spiral. The dataset records whorl expansion rate W (Raup-type), so alpha = arctan(2π/ln W) per whorl. Check: W = 3 for Nautilus gives alpha of about 80°, matching Thompson. This tests only the gastropod part of the claim, because the dataset has no ammonoids or Nautilus. This is a restriction to a subset of the claim's scope and a modern reinterpretation. The dataset's "helicospiral" models also include translation along the axis, so the spiral angle is taken from the projected expansion rate only. The exact column names in the CSV were not visible on the landing page and must be confirmed.

dataset.publisher: Dryad (Collins, Klapaukh, Crampton, Gazley, Schipper, Maksimenko, Hines)
dataset.why_it_fits: It gives best-fit coiling parameters, including whorl expansion rate, for 176 fossil and modern gastropod shells. The files are S_Table_3_hangle_output.csv, S_Table_1_Specimens.csv, S_Table_2_metadata.csv and the Rmd processing scripts. The expansion rate converts directly to the logarithmic-spiral constant angle.
